title: File input and output

youtube.title: C++ File I/O: ifstream and ofstream | C++ Programming EP 83
youtube.description: In this episode you will write text to a file, read lines from a file and check that a file opened, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 File input and output · 1:00 Write then read lines · 2:15 Stream directions · 2:47 Second program · 4:16 Recap · 4:46 Bug of the Day · 5:35 Challenge · 6:02 Next episode

thumbnail.visual: big text "FILES" in tomato on cream; Xecxec next to a notebook being written, closed and read back; thin black border and drop shadow.
thumbnail.pose: Xecxec next to a notebook being written, closed and read back

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we save data in files. A file keeps its data after the program ends, so you can read it again later.

scenes.onScreen: "File input and output": numbered lines (1. Ofstream writes to a file; 2. Ifstream reads from a file; 3. Always check that the file opened) and an analogy card: a notebook you write in, close, and open again later
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: Ofstream writes to a file. Ifstream reads from a file. You use them like cout and cin. Think of a notebook. You write in it, close it, and open it again later. Variables vanish when the program ends. Files stay. If you want to keep data, you save it in a file. File streams use the same arrows as cout and cin. If you know how to print and read, you already know how to use files.
points: Always check that the file opened

analogy.title: File input and output
analogy.body: A notebook you write in, close, and open again later

scenes.onScreen: files.cpp: two lines are written to a file, then read back
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 8] Ofstream opens the file for writing. It makes the file if it does not exist. [HL 9] We write to it with the insert operator, like cout. [HL 11] Close saves the data. [HL 13] Ifstream opens the same file for reading. [HL 15] Getline reads one line at a time. The loop stops at the end of the file. [HL 16] We print Asha ninety-one, and Ravi seventy-eight. [HL 19] Remove deletes the file, to keep the folder clean. [HL 8] This line makes an output stream and opens the file. If the file does not exist, the stream creates it. [HL 9] The arrows send the text into the file, and the backslash n ends the line. [HL 11] Close writes the last data to the disk. [HL 13] An input stream opens the same file. [HL 15] Getline reads one full line at a time, until the file ends.

scenes.onScreen: a table of the two stream types
scenes.animation: Table rows slide in one by one; the row the narrator mentions glows butter
scenes.narration: Ofstream sends data from the program to a file, like cout. Ifstream brings data from a file into the program, like cin. Fstream can do both. Notice the three steps. Open the stream, use it, and close it. The stream is like a pipe between your program and the file on the disk.

diagram.caption: a table of the two stream types

scenes.onScreen: marks.cpp: a file of names and marks is added up
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 8] We write three names with marks into a file. [HL 16] The extraction operator reads one word and then one number. It works like cin. The loop ends when a read fails, at the end of the file. [HL 17] Each mark goes into the total. [HL 19] The total is ninety-one plus seventy-eight plus eighty-five, which is two hundred and fifty-four. [HL 9] All the data sits on one line, with spaces between the items. [HL 16] The arrows read a word and a number each time. The loop stops when the reading fails. [HL 17] Each mark is added to the total. Ninety-one plus seventy-eight plus eighty-five makes two hundred and fifty-four.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as marks dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints Asha ninety-one, Ravi seventy-eight, and then two hundred and fifty-four. Check by hand. Ninety-one plus seventy-eight is one hundred sixty-nine. Add eighty-five, and the total is two hundred fifty-four.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. Ofstream writes to a file. Two. Ifstream reads from a file. Three. Getline reads a whole line. Four. Check that the file opened. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: A file that did not open
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; the program runs and the wrong output appears in tomato; the fix slides in and the output turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. The file does not exist, but the program prints First line and nothing else. No error shows up. Always check that the file opened. A file stream that fails to open does not shout. It stays in a failed state, and every read gives nothing. So test the stream right after you open it. Check the file name, and the folder where the program runs.

scenes.onScreen: Why did the file feel safe? Someone always closed it properly.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: Why did the file feel safe? Someone always closed it properly.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: count the lines in a file
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Write a program that saves three lines to a file. Then read them back, and print how many lines you found. Hint: read the file with getline, and add one to a counter for each line. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.onScreen: Next: EP 84 · Namespaces and organising code
scenes.animation: Next-episode card slides up with a whoosh; right side stays empty for end-screen elements; sign-off text types in
scenes.narration: Next time: namespaces and organising code. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
